body:
## Summary
Implements #68: the budget circuit breaker was throwing on $0 operations.

- `CostTracker.trackOperation` now computes cost **before** the breaker check and throws only for paid operations (`cost > 0`). Cache hits (`cached === true` → cost 0) and free providers (Ollama, pricing 0) always proceed and are still recorded.
- `SmartAIVisionClient.analyzeVisualDiff`'s pre-attempt budget check now applies only to paid providers (`getPricing(provider, model) > 0`), so free local Ollama is never blocked in the fallback chain.
- The cache-hit `trackOperation(..., true)` call stays uncaught — it can no longer throw, so cached results are returned instead of being silently replaced by the classifier's wrong `unknown/medium` fallback.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] Circuit-breaker check skipped when `cached === true` (via `cost > 0` gate; `computeCost` returns 0 for cached)
- [x] Pre-call breaker applies only to paid providers (pricing > 0)
- [x] Cache-hit path never fails on budget status
- [x] Tests for cache-hit and Ollama under exhausted budget (unit + integration)
- [x] Paid providers still blocked when the breaker is triggered

## Test Plan
- [x] Unit tests written first (TDD): 4 new tests failed on the production bug before the fix
- [x] All tests passing (full suite: 745 passed, 1 skipped; ai-client-batch4: 39/39)
- [x] Diff coverage 100% on changed lines (diff-cover vs origin/main, gate ≥85%)
- [x] Linting clean (1 pre-existing warning in unrelated `visual-runner.test.ts`)
- [x] Internal code review (advisory): APPROVE
- [x] Cross-family review pass: opencode (GLM): APPROVE
- [x] Test mutation sanity check: 3 mutations (always-throw gate, never-throw gate, universal pre-check) each killed by the new tests

## Known Limitations / Intentionally Deferred
- "Paid" is keyed on the flat per-image price: a custom model registered with `costPerImage: 0` but token rates > 0 would skip the *pre-call* gate (the post-call `trackOperation` breaker still fires). Not reachable with default pricing; documented inline in `smart-client.ts`. Both cross-family review findings were about this edge and were resolved by documentation per the reviewer's suggestion.
- Unpriced custom models (`getPricing` = 0) are treated as free and not budget-gated — pre-existing semantics of the pricing map, unchanged by this PR.

## Implementation Notes
- Existing test "throws when the budget circuit breaker is tripped" configured provider `openai` but inherited model `llava` from the shared mock config — pricing 0, so under the corrected semantics it would (rightly) not be blocked. The fixture now uses the explicitly paid `gpt-4o`, preserving the test's intent; explained inline.
- Gate uses `cost > 0` alone (not `!cached && cost > 0`): `computeCost` returns 0 for cached ops, so the extra term is redundant.

Closes #68

body:
> **Stacked on #111** (`fix/bot-click-analytics`) — both touch `apps/etl`. Merge #111 first, then retarget/merge this one; the diff shown against `main` includes #111's commit until then.

Implements **PR1 of `.scratch/cv-match-flow-design.md`** (§1.1 role suggester, §1.2 role filter, §6/§8 calibration instrumentation).

## Role suggester — `GET /cv/:id/role-suggestions`

- Scores every VERIFIED ROLE node by the share of its last-30d eligible vacancies the candidate's skill set covers at GOOD+ (`FIT_GOOD_MIN`), reusing the matcher's IDF-weighted coverage machinery: the `cand/css/ov/agg` aggregation CTEs are **extracted into a shared `coverageCtes()`** (plus a `scored` step computing the coverage ratio) consumed by both `rankByRefs` and `suggestRoles` — no duplicated SQL. `rankByRefs`' `tier_bucket` now derives from that same coverage column (behavior-identical CASE).
- Laplace smoothing `(good+1)/(total+4)` for ordering; floors `total >= 10` and `score >= 0.05`; top-5 sorted `score DESC, total DESC, name`; the CV's declared role (via `resolveRole`) pinned first with its honest score; response items carry `goodCount/totalCount` numerators for UI credibility.
- Cold start: when no role clears the floor, items re-rank by mean weighted coverage and the response is flagged `reduced: true` (same query, second aggregate column).
- Selection/smoothing math is a pure function (`role-suggestions.derive.ts`) with an 8-case spec, mirroring the existing `recommendation.derive` pattern.
- Public sample twin `GET /cv/samples/:id/role-suggestions` mirrors `samples/:id/matches` so the anonymous sample-profile flow gets suggestions too.

### ⚠️ One deliberate deviation from the doc

The doc floors the **Laplace score** at 0.05 — but with `total >= 10` the smoothed score can never drop below 1/14 ≈ 0.071, so that floor is mathematically dead: 0-good roles would always show and `reduced` could never trigger. Verified against a local prod copy: 10-vacancy/0-good roles outranked a 10-good/164 role. **The floor here tests the raw GOOD+ share (`good/total >= 0.05`); Laplace still orders.** This preserves every stated intent (smoothing prevents small-sample domination, floor marks "not yours", cold-start fallback is reachable). Spec-locked with a dedicated test; happy to flip back if you prefer the literal formula.

## Role hard filter

- `MatchFilters.roleNodeIds` (OR, hard filter — explicit user choice, unlike the inferred `on_stack` demote) → one `buildFilters` condition mirroring `domainIds`.
- Plumbed as ROLE slugs: `roleIds` CSV on `GET /cv/:id/matches` + `GET /cv/samples/:id/matches`, `roleIds[]` on `POST /ranking/match` (`MatchDto`), resolved server-side via `NodeSlugResolver`.
- Web: `warm-query`/`warmFilterKey` carry `filters.roleIds` (already URL-synced as `?roles=` by the shared codec); the warm sidebar gains a searchable **role multiselect** (shared `FilterRail`, warm-only like `min fit`) where suggested roles lead with `name · N/M fit` labels and the full catalog stays searchable; `useRoleSuggestions` preselects the top-3 suggested slugs **once per candidate** when the URL has no explicit `?roles=` (a reduced result never preselects; clearing chips doesn't resurrect them).

## Instrumentation (§8 calibration)

- `match_scored` server-side PostHog event (personless, `$process_person_profile: false`): 10-bucket coverage histogram + tier counts over the filtered result set, emitted fire-and-forget on page-1 requests only (every fresh match starts at page 1 — natural sampling). Falls out of the shared `ranked` CTE, one extra aggregate query.
- Client-side flow events from §6 (`role_selected`, `role_suggestions_shown`, …) are **deferred** — they belong to the `/match` stepper (doc PR4); nothing in this PR's UI is unmeasurable server-side.

## Verification

- `pnpm build` (database + etl), `pnpm build:web`, `pnpm lint` (etl + web): all pass.
- `pnpm --filter @metahunt/etl test`: 368 passed (incl. the new derive spec); `pnpm test:web`: 54 passed.
- Suggester SQL smoke-tested against a local prod-copy DB with a NestJS/Node/PostgreSQL/TypeScript profile — sane totals/good counts, Full Stack Developer surfacing at 10/164.

Docs: `md/architecture/overview.md` CvModule paragraph updated; release note in `md/journal/releases.md`.

💡 What:
Optimized the `_get_title` method in `GuardianAgent` to directly use $O(1)$ dictionary lookup checks (`.get()`) for common property keys (`"Name"`, `"Entry"`, `"title"`, `"rich_text"`) instead of performing linear searches and throwing/catching exceptions on mock/benchmark Notion properties.
Also updated Python benchmark tests (`benchmark_bolt.py`, `benchmark_collaborative.py`, `benchmark_guardian.py`, `benchmark_guardian_hoist.py`) to patch the correct original source paths (`src.antigravity_core.notion_client.NotionClient` and `src.antigravity_core.gemini_client.GeminiClient`), resolving patching errors from lazy-loaded application logic.

🎯 Why:
The original implementation of `_get_title` performed a linear loop using a generator expression that expected `v["id"] == "title"`. When evaluating mock or custom property dictionaries that did not contain the `"id"` key, this raised a `KeyError` which was silently caught, causing the method to return `"Error extracting title"` for all titles.
This exception-raising-and-catching cycle occurred on every single title lookup during test runs and benchmarks, adding massive execution-handling latency and breaking title extraction correctness in mock/benchmark environments.

📊 Impact:
- Reduces latency of `_get_title` under mock/benchmark environments by ~61% (latency dropped from 0.0816s to 0.0318s for 50,000 iterations).
- Resolves the correctness bug: title extraction now successfully returns the correct title content instead of `"Error extracting title"`.
- Enables all benchmark tests to run successfully and securely without real-world API dependency leakage.

Reworks the model shipped in #175. No schema change: the two Assets fields are reused with different meaning, and there is no live data to migrate since the old entry point was never reachable in practice.

**Before:** `variantOf` held a base map's asset id. That made one map load bearing for the others, so renaming or removing the base orphaned its faces, and filing was a pairwise "this is a face of that" which read backwards.

**Now:** `variantOf` holds a group name the LM types (`The Bridge`); `variantLabel` holds the face name (`Broken`). Maps sharing a group name are peers. `mapGroup`, `mapGroups`, `mapsInGroup` and `mapFamily` all derive from the string, so no map is special and removing any one leaves the rest intact.

author: bejoyfuuul
body:
The non-agent promotion channel for L1, on top of the schema (#110) and the ledger changes (#111). This is what lets a CI check contribute to promoting knowledge to `trusted` - and the demotion path that lets an agent flag a fact as wrong without ever being able to promote one.

## Why this endpoint exists at all

An agent authenticates with a connect code. If a connect code could promote knowledge, an agent could manufacture its own trusted facts and spread them to every other agent's `recall`. So promotion lives on a **separate HTTP route with its own per-project secret**, never handed to an agent. `POST /api/knowledge/attest` is not an MCP tool; a connect code cannot reach it.

The endpoint does not decide promotion. It verifies a signal and hands it to the shared ledger function, which counts the whole CI system as **one issuer** - so two CI attestations alone never reach K=2. Reaching trusted without a human owner override needs a second distinct principal.

## Validation order is load-bearing

```
format  400  shape + assertion (an unknown assertion is refused, not waved through)
auth    401  key selected by keyId; missing project, null secret, and key mismatch are ALL 401
skew    400  issuedAt within a symmetric window; the future is refused too
tenant  404  the claim must belong to the signing project - checked BEFORE the nonce is spent
replay  409  a validly-signed request is spendable once; a duplicate (project_id, nonce) is the replay
```

Two of these orderings are deliberate, not incidental:

- **Every auth failure is 401, including a project that never enabled attestation.** A 404 there would leak whether a project has attestation turned on. Missing project, null secret, and wrong key are indistinguishable from outside.
- **The tenant check precedes the nonce insert.** A request pointed at another project's claim gets 404 without burning a nonce - a forged or misdirected request must not be able to spend nonces it never earned.

## validationId without a re-query

The response contract is `{ validationId, counted }`, and both come straight from the ledger function's result - no read from outside its transaction. The locally-computed `counted` only decides what the *first* insert stores; the response returns the **stored** value. So a replay (same run, new nonce) returns the original validation id and the original `counted`, even if the check-map was deleted in between. Three tests pin that.

## Demotion: the safe direction, with provenance

An `event` of `type: 'error'` carrying `detail.contradicts: <knowledgeId>` records a contradiction against that entry. It rides the event row, so the demotion carries its reason (the error event itself) rather than appearing from nowhere.

- **No payload can promote.** The signal is fixed to `contradict`; a test sends `detail.signal: 'support'` and the entry still ends `contradicted`.
- **A contradiction that cannot apply is reported, not swallowed** - `contradiction: {applied: false, reason}`. Unknown id and another project's id are answered identically, because the ledger answers them identically and distinguishing them here would leak existence.
- **Rate-limited** through the same gate as `learn`, so an agent cannot loop demotions to retire trusted entries.

## The invariant, proven through the real endpoint

The core function guarantees "two CI attestations alone do not reach K=2", but this asserts it through an actual signed request path:

```
✓ TWO CI attestations alone do NOT reach K=2 (one issuer)  -> stays candidate
✓ ONE CI + ONE human (two issuers)                          -> trusted
```

Two negative controls: forcing `counted=true` regardless of the map fails the unmapped test; removing the nonce check fails the replay test. Plus forged-signature 401 (and nothing recorded), disabled-project 401, a rotated key dying past its grace window, a forgery failing to spend a nonce so a later genuine request still succeeds, and cross-project 404.

## Testing

`apps/server`: 269 across 32 files. New: endpoint 15, contradiction 7, canonical 8, skew 6. The `tools/list` snapshot changed by one line (the `event` tool's detail description), so the tool-contract diff stays reviewable.

author: feodorfitsner
body:
## Summary

A system/edge-swipe **back** gesture that lands on an **embedded `FletApp`** (an app rendered inside another Flet app via `FletApp` — e.g. a gallery host running example apps in-process) closed the whole host app instead of navigating back.

## Root cause

This is Android's **predictive-back** path, not the legacy `didPopRoute` path.

Every `WidgetsApp` (`MaterialApp`/`CupertinoApp`) listens for `NavigationNotification`, and its default handler both calls `SystemNavigator.setFrameworkHandlesBack(canHandlePop)` and **stops** the notification. The embedded example's single-view `Navigator` reports `canHandlePop: false`, so the embedded `WidgetsApp`:

1. told the OS the framework does **not** handle back, and
2. swallowed the notification before it could reach the **host** `Navigator` — which would have re-reported `canHandlePop: true`, since it can pop the view embedding the app.

The OS then finished the activity → the app exits. `didPopRoute` never fired.

## Fix

For an embedded page (`backend.controlId != null`), in `packages/flet/lib/src/controls/page.dart`:

- **`onNavigationNotification: (_) => false`** — don't run `WidgetsApp`'s default handler; let the notification bubble to the host, whose `Navigator` re-reports `canHandlePop: true` and whose `WidgetsApp` calls `setFrameworkHandlesBack(true)`. This is what stops the OS from finishing the activity.
- **`ChildBackButtonDispatcher`** chained to the host `Router` (instead of the default `RootBackButtonDispatcher`) — so once back actually reaches `didPopRoute`, an unhandled back propagates from the embedded `Router` to the host `Router`, which pops the view embedding the `FletApp`. This also preserves correct precedence for multi-view embedded apps: they pop their own inner view first, then fall through to the host.

Non-embedded (root) pages are unaffected: `onNavigationNotification` stays `null` (default handler) and no child dispatcher is created.

## Testing

- Verified on a real Android device (moto g15) and on an emulator: back-swipe on an embedded example now returns to the host view instead of exiting the app.
- Verified against Flutter 3.44.7 source for both the `NavigationNotification` combining logic (`Navigator`) and the dispatcher fall-through (`BackButtonDispatcher`/`ChildBackButtonDispatcher`).
- `flutter analyze` clean.

## Notes

This makes an embedded app defer back-reporting to its host, which is correct for the only way `FletApp` embeds today (inside another Flet app with its own `Navigator`).

## Summary by Sourcery

Ensure embedded Flet apps delegate system back handling to their host so edge-swipe back navigates within the host instead of exiting the entire app.

Bug Fixes:
- Prevent Android system/edge-swipe back gestures on embedded FletApp pages from closing the host app by propagating back events to the host navigator.

Documentation:
- Document the embedded FletApp back gesture fix in the main changelog and package changelog for version 0.86.3.

## Problem

Sandbox Mode today is a single global toggle on Ghost Settings. Turning it
on returns the fixed OTP for **every** request on the site — real users
included. That makes it unsafe to enable for load/QA testing against a
site with any real traffic, since real logins would silently break.

## What this adds

An independent, narrower trigger: **Sandbox Email Domain**. When set,
only OTP requests whose email ends in that domain get the fixed OTP (no
real send, no DB record) — every other email still goes through real OTP
generation and delivery, unaffected.

- Global `sandbox_mode` keeps working exactly as before, for full dev/QA
  environments with no real traffic.
- The new field is opt-in and blank by default — no behavior change for
  anyone not using it.
- `_is_sandboxed(settings, email)` is shared by `generate()` and
  `verify()` so both stay in sync.

- `email=probe@loadtest.internal` (with `sandbox_email_domain` set to

  delivery.
- `email=realuser@gmail.com` (non-matching domain) → real random OTP,
  `sent: true`, real delivery attempted — unaffected by the sandbox
  config.

Came out of load-testing `beta.gohoppily.com`'s backend

- **`resolveTitleCategoryRef(payableId)`** (composition): `payableDocView.findByPayableIds([payableId])` → `categoryRef` (mesmo port do `export-reconciliation-nibo`). Graceful → null.
- **Handler**: `categoryRef = manualEntry?.categoryRef ?? (items[0] ? resolveTitleCategoryRef(payableId) : null)` → nome via `resolveCategoryName` (fatia 1). **Lançamento manual tem precedência** (não regride).

body:
This is a cross-fork follow-up based directly on `Hixie:fuse-list-all-space-pieces`, so merging it updates #4894 without transferring ownership of the original PR.

## What this resolves

- Adds a persistent `entitySetSeq` that changes only when live default-branch, space-scoped entity membership changes. Value-only writes no longer starve long listings; add/delete/resurrection still invalidate them.
- Makes continuation requests require both `after` and `expectedEntitySetSeq`.
- Caps list responses at 1,000 IDs, 256 KiB of serialized identifier data, and 16 KiB per ID.
- Coalesces concurrent enumeration and shares one immutable snapshot between compatible directory handles.
- Enforces a 64 MiB estimated resident-snapshot budget, including old generations pinned by open handles.
- Maps membership races to `EAGAIN` and other preparation failures to `EIO`, rather than making `entities/` appear missing.
- Exposes current and high-water projection/snapshot retention in `.status`.
- Deprecates the aggregate runner listing helper in favor of the paged API.
- Corrects the Memory/FUSE/path documentation and renames the misleading historical `stubs-*` benchmark series.

## Regression evidence

The benchmark now uses the same lookup/forget state machine as the FUSE callbacks:

- 100k retained lookup replies: 100,008 inodes, ~110 MiB V8 heap, 965–986 ms.
- 100k lookup+forget pairs: 136 inodes / 128 retained roots, 1.61–1.67 s.

Shared enumeration over 100k IDs:

- 1 handle: 100 pages, ~5.5 MiB wire, ~6.5 MiB heap, 247–249 ms.
- 10 handles: the same 100 pages/wire/heap, 240–244 ms.
- 100 handles: the same 100 pages/wire/heap, 239–263 ms.

Storage on the 100k-live fixture:

- first/continuation 1,000-ID page: ~165–168 µs;
- complete 100-page traversal: ~16.3 ms;
- exact existence hit: ~5.4 µs.

The existing real-mount benchmark harness also has an `entity_find` operation. It runs the host `find` command and captures `.status` before/after; high-water counters preserve peak retention even if kernel `forget` arrives before the final sample.

## Verification

- Focused Memory/Runner/FUSE suites: 248 passed.
- Documentation: all 520 checked code blocks passed.
- Repository check: all 400 paths type-checked.
- Benchmark source and real-mount harness type-check.

## Deliberate boundary

Kernel-referenced inode roots cannot be hard-evicted safely. This change makes that case explicit and observable, keeps roots identifier-only, and reclaims them after `forget`. A compact virtual-inode representation or independent hydrated-descendant budget remains a larger follow-up if real mounted `find` results show the current lightweight root cost is still unacceptable.

## Summary

- detect exact graph-scoped KA page replays that are already durably materialized
- verify the locally stored assertion identity, confirmation markers, and recomputed V10 content root before using the fast path
- preserve normal on-chain authentication for every new, changed, incomplete, malformed, or mismatched asset

## Live evidence

During testnet durable sync, a large page could materialize early KAs and then miss the graph deadline while authenticating a later KA. Because the page checkpoint correctly remained unadvanced, the next attempt authenticated every already committed KA again before reaching the tail. This change makes those exact replays local-store work instead of repeated RPC work.

## Security boundary

This is an optimization only. The replay probe requires one immutable root, exact assertion version and graph bindings, trusted local materializedVersion and confirmed markers, and a recomputation of the stored assertion V10 root. Any ambiguity or mismatch falls through to the existing chain-authenticated path.

author: lezama
body:
## The failure

An end-to-end run that activated a generated theme on a real WordPress site took the whole site down. The generated `fonts.php` opened with what the model clearly meant as a self-inclusion guard:

```php
require_once __DIR__ . '/fonts.php' === __FILE__ ? '' : '';
```

`.` binds tighter than `===`, so this parses as `require_once ( (__DIR__ . '/fonts.php') === __FILE__ ? '' : '' )` — both branches yield `''`, making it **`require_once ''`**: a fatal on every single load.

```
Warning: require_once(): Failed to open stream: No such file or directory in …/fonts.php on line 13
Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Failed opening required ''
```

Because `functions.php` requires `fonts.php` on every request, the site fataled the moment the theme became active — including WP-CLI, so `wp theme activate` could no longer switch away from it. Recovery needed `wp --skip-themes --skip-plugins option update stylesheet …`.

## Why validation missed it

`validate()` ends with `php -l`, and this line is **syntactically valid** — the failure is at runtime. Structure, hooks, URLs and scan coverage all passed too, so the model's file shipped instead of the deterministic fallback.

## The fix

`fonts.php` enqueues styles and nothing else — it has no legitimate reason to include a file. Rejecting `require`/`include` (any form) closes this whole class of lint-invisible runtime fatal, and the existing fallback path takes over exactly as designed.

The pattern is anchored so identifiers and words that merely contain them (`requirements:`, `$this->require_once`) stay valid — covered by a test.

## Tests

New case in `fonts_php_test.php`: the real self-inclusion guard is rejected, plain `require`/`include_once` are rejected, and a comment containing "requirements" still validates. `12 passed, 0 failed` for the fonts suite.

Note: `php tests/run.php` currently dies partway through on trunk with `Cannot redeclare builder_content_activate()` (pre-existing, unrelated to this change) — the fonts file was run in isolation.

body:
## macOS Research menu — Switch Project + New Project

Implements the design pivot from PR #458 (closed): the project switcher belongs in the **Research menu**, always reachable from any window, as a pure active-project re-scope — not tied to Project Home's per-project window.

### What's added (macOS-only)
**Research ▸ Switch Project ▸** — a submenu with:
- **Global Context** + a **live, checkmarked list of every project**. Picking one **purely re-scopes** the app (sets the active project → the Working-on banner, search scope, and leads follow it). **No window opens.** The checkmark tracks the active project.
- **Manage Projects…** — opens Settings landed directly on the **Projects** pane (rename / merge / delete / create).

**Research ▸ New Project…** — opens `ProjectEditorView` in a small window (a menu command can't present a sheet). Save creates the project (it appears live in the switcher) and closes the window.

### How it works (grounded in existing patterns)
- The live project list is a `@Query` in a small `ProjectSwitcherMenuContent` view, resolving via the **same `.modelContainer` injection the sibling History submenu already uses** — so it stays live (create / rename / delete) with **no `AppState` project cache**.
- "Manage Projects…" sets a transient `AppState.pendingSettingsPaneRaw` before `openSettings()`; `FRUSSettingsView` consumes it (`.task` + `.onChange`) to select the Projects pane — the exact idiom `MacCollectionManagerView` already uses for `pendingCollectionSelection`.
- The New Project window closes via `dismiss()`, the **same mechanism the Note Composer window uses** (`ResearchNoteEditorView`). The editor gains a `showsInlineHeader` flag (default `true`) so the window drops the internal title that would duplicate its titlebar; the two existing sheet callers are unchanged.

### Adversarial review (folded)
Confirmed sound: the `@Query` liveness/container injection, the pending-pane consume logic (no race/double-consume), `openSettings` threading, checkmark rendering, `showsInlineHeader` back-compat, macOS-only confinement, and clean builds on both platforms.

**Documented (not fixed) — deliberate:** the once-ever **second-project nudge won't fire** when the 2nd project is created via this new **New Project window** — the transient window dismisses on Save and isn't a nudge host. Mounting the nudge on the multi-instance main window would reintroduce the multi-fire the #456 review specifically guarded against, so the nudge stays best-effort/host-dependent (it still fires from the iOS "+" and the macOS Settings pane). Same limitation already noted for the Project Home create path.

Both platforms build (`FRUSExplorerMac` + `FRUSExplorer` iOS — the shared `AppState`/`ProjectEditorView` changes compile clean on iOS).

---

## Visual-review checklist (owner verifies on-device, macOS)
- [ ] **Research ▸ Switch Project** shows **Global Context** + all projects; the **checkmark** sits on the current one and **moves** when you pick another. Picking a project **re-scopes** (check the Browse/Search "Working on:" banner) and **opens no window**.
- [ ] Create/rename/delete a project → the submenu list updates **live**.
- [ ] **Switch Project ▸ Manage Projects…** opens Settings **on the Projects pane** (both when Settings is closed and when it's already open on another pane).
- [ ] **Research ▸ New Project…** opens the small window (titlebar "New Project", no duplicate inline title). **Save** creates the project (appears in the switcher) and **closes** the window; **Cancel** closes it too. Reopening gives a fresh blank form.

author: cov12
body:
Two backend fixes found while diagnosing a "dashboard shows another org's sub-account" report. (That report itself was a **session-switch** issue — the browser kept a stale OWUI session from a previous account; the auth gates held and no data crossed tenants — tracked as its own focused PR.)

## 1. `_extract_list` mis-parses an org with 0 sub-accounts
Portal returns `{"subAccounts": []}` for an org with no sub-accounts. The `data.get("subAccounts") or data.get("subaccounts")` idiom treats the **empty list as falsy**, so it fell through to `None` → logged `unexpected Portal payload shape` → the login-sync no-op'd. Fix: select the wrapper key by **presence**, so `[]` means "no sub-accounts," not "absent/unexpected."

## 2. Refuse cross-tenant row reassignment (defense-in-depth)
`sync_org_subaccounts` matched the upsert target by **global `id`** and reassigned `row.org_id`. Portal ids are globally unique and each org syncs only its own, so this never fired in practice — but a mismatched `(org, token)` call could **move a row across tenants**. Added a guard: refuse to reassign a row whose `portal_org_id` belongs to a **different** Portal org. A re-provision under a new AgencyOS internal id keeps the **same** `portal_org_id`, so that legit case still updates.

## Tests
`{"subAccounts": []}` / `{"data": []}` / `[]` all parse as `[]`; a cross-tenant sync cannot steal another org's row (binding stays put, no bogus copy). Full suite green.

body: Closes ENG-522. Folds in ENG-362 (GPLv3 relicense). Nothing in this workspace was released anywhere. `templar-backend/services/blockchain-gateway` pins seven crates to a raw `dev` commit because no release tag contains `gateway/`; tags used three naming schemes; the only GitHub Release was a draft. `contract/artifacts` stored one WASM blob per contract, overwritten in place — so `gateway/testing/src/wasm.rs` hand-hoarded five historical blobs as ad-hoc `include_bytes!` consts, outside the catalog and outside any drift check. ## What this adds **Per-crate releases via release-plz.** Every crate versions itself from its own commit history. Merging the standing "chore: release" PR is the trigger; an ordinary merge to `dev` ships nothing. Three tiers: published (the 17-crate closure consumers import), tagged-only (contracts, services, tools), internal (mocks, fuzz, scaffolding). **Released WASM as GitHub Release assets.** Bytes are no longer repository content. `release-artifacts.yml` builds the contract reproducibly **at the release tag's own commit**, attaches the WASM plus `checksums.txt` to the Release, and opens a PR appending one row to `contract/artifacts/releases.tsv`. Consumers fetch into a shared out-of-repo cache (`just artifacts-fetch`) and verify against the SHA-256 pinned in that row. **Commit conventions**, documented in AGENTS.md and enforced by a PR-title lint, since squash-merge makes the PR title the commit that drives version inference. ## The finding that shaped this **A release means the bytes were deployed, not that a version was bumped.** The old catalog keyed off each crate's `Cargo.toml` version, and those diverge routinely — market reached 1.4.0 while 1.3.0 was the newest deployment, registry 1.2.1 against a deployed 1.1.0. Checked against the accounts actually running the code, **ten of twelve `res/` blobs had never been on chain**, and four versions had same-number-different-bytes. The catalog now records what shipped — which only CI can know, after the fact. 17 real releases replaced 9 fictional ones. That principle is applied consistently, not just to the version: **every field of a release record is observed, never derived.** - The **tag** and **asset** are recorded as CI saw them. They name objects that already exist on GitHub, and this repo has used three tag schemes over its life — 7 of 81 tags still don't match the current one. Reconstructing them from release-plz's `git_tag_name` template would assume a uniformity that has never held, and would strand every old release the moment that template changed. - The **version** comes from the crate's own `Cargo.toml` at the tag, which release-plz set moments earlier — authoritative, rather than parsed back out of a tag string. - The **digest** is of the bytes CI just built. So the release history is data, in a five-column TSV compiled in by `build.rs`. A release PR diffs as exactly the row added; a malformed row fails the build; an unknown artifact id fails to *compile*, because it generates a match arm for a variant that doesn't exist. ## Why the build happens at the tag `cargo near build reproducible-wasm` embeds its source commit per NEP-330; nearblocks.io/SourceScan reads that commit back off a *deployed* contract, clones at it, and rebuilds. A squash-merged feature branch never becomes an ancestor of `dev` and is eventually garbage-collected — so a blob built on a branch is one gc away from being unverifiable by anyone. A tag is reachable from a fresh clone forever. This also settles the fixpoint problem: a reproducible build's hash cannot be written into the commit that produces it, so the catalog row necessarily lands one commit later. ## Backfill (already run) The 17 historical releases were recovered from the chain — bytes read off the accounts running them, each tagged at the commit its own metadata names — so they reproduce on the same terms as future ones. Tags, Releases and assets are live, and every recorded tag and asset was verified against the real GitHub Releases before being committed. Four of those build commits survived on a single branch each; deleting that branch would have made deployed mainnet code permanently unverifiable. The provenance table is recorded in a comment on this PR. ## Things worth knowing **crates.io publishing is configured but deferred.** `templar-common` depends on the RedStone SDK as a git dependency, and Cargo refuses to publish any crate with one. author: aparajon
body:
## Why this matters

`schemabot logs -n 50` claimed to show recent logs but actually returned the *oldest* 50 entries: the storage read ordered ascending and applied the limit there. For any apply with more than N log lines — exactly the applies an operator is triaging — the command silently showed the beginning of the story and none of the current state. The newest entries, the ones that answer "what is it doing right now", were unreachable no matter what `-n` you passed.

## What it does

`logs -n` now returns the newest N entries, still printed oldest-first within the window (standard tail semantics). The storage read selects the newest window (`ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC` with the limit, then reversed for delivery), with the write-ordered id as tie-break so same-second entries cannot shuffle. The remote data-plane read path already had these semantics; this aligns the control-plane path with it.

It also adds `--follow` for apply and deployment logs (folded in from #821): after printing the initial window, the command polls for new entries and streams them as they land, so an operator can watch a live apply instead of re-running the command.

## How it moves us toward the northstar

`logs` is the first tool an operator reaches for when an apply looks stuck. It has to answer "what happened most recently" by default — a log window that ends where the incident begins is worse than no window at all — and `--follow` keeps answering it as the apply progresses.

author: dichovsky
body:
## Summary

Makes page rendering measurably faster with zero output change — all rendered PNGs are **byte-identical** to the previous build (verified across all 37 pages of the three benchmark PDFs), no public defaults change, no new dependencies.

### What was slow (measured, not guessed)

A new committed benchmark (`npm run bench`) plus CPU profiling attributed the cost per document class:

| Document | render | PNG encode |
|---|---|---|
| `large_pdf.pdf` (12p, ~7.6 MP JPEGs) | 95.4% | 4.6% |
| `TAMReview.pdf` (23p, text-heavy) | 36.8% | **62.8%** |
| `sample.pdf` (2p) | 18.3% | **80.3%** |

For typical text documents, the synchronous `canvas.toBuffer('image/png')` dominated — and it blocks the event loop, so nothing (not even disk writes) overlapped it. `large_pdf` is the outlier: its four image pages spend ~65% of render inside pdf.js's main-thread `convertRGBToRGBA` and ~20% in its pure-JS JPEG decoder (see follow-ups).

### Changes

1. **Async off-thread PNG encode** — `canvas.toBuffer('image/png')` → `await canvas.encode('png')` (`src/pageRenderer.ts`). Same native Skia encoder, byte-identical output, but encoding now runs on the libuv threadpool and the JS thread is free to render the next page.
2. **Sequential mode pipelines** — sequential (default) conversions now run through the existing sliding-window helper with a fixed window of 2 (`SEQUENTIAL_PIPELINE_WINDOW`), so page N's encode/disk-write overlaps page N+1's render. Output order unchanged; at most one extra canvas alive.
3. **Zero-copy input handoff** — the `readFile` branch of `getPdfFileBuffer` no longer copies the whole file; the library-owned buffer is handed to pdf.js as a full-span view (guarded, with copy fallback), which pdf.js transfers without copying.
4. **Committed benchmark** — `scripts/benchmark.ts` + `npm run bench`: end-to-end scenarios (sequential/parallel × buffer/file × 3 documents) and a per-stage breakdown (load/getPage/render/encode), 5 iterations + warmup, results saved as JSON under `bench-results/` (gitignored).

### Results (median of 5, Node v22.23.1, darwin/arm64, Apple Silicon)

| Scenario | Before | After | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAMReview (23p) → buffers, sequential | 1396.3 ms | 834.8 ms | **−40.2%** |
| sample (2p) → buffers, sequential | 44.4 ms | 28.4 ms | **−36.0%** |
| large_pdf (12p) → files, parallel(4) | 12007.9 ms | 10600.7 ms | **−11.7%** |
| large_pdf (12p) → buffers, parallel(4) | 11685.8 ms | 10700.2 ms | **−8.4%** |
| large_pdf (12p) → files, sequential | 11928.0 ms | 11476.3 ms | −3.8% |
| large_pdf (12p) → buffers, sequential | 11714.4 ms | 11358.3 ms | −3.0% |

## Verification

- **Byte-identity:** all 37 output PNGs (`large_pdf`, `TAMReview`, `sample`) byte-compared before vs after — identical.
- `npm run build:test`, `npm run build:strict`, `npm run lint`, `npm run codemap` — clean.
- Full test suite: 41 files / 224 passed, 2 skipped.
- New tests: sequential window-2 pipelining + order preservation; zero-copy handoff + pooled-buffer copy fallback.
- Multi-agent adversarial review of the diff (async correctness, buffer safety, API compat, test quality): 17 raw findings, 11 confirmed after adversarial verification, all addressed:
  - **Fixed in code:** stale public JSDoc promising one-at-a-time sequential processing (HIGH); nondeterministic error selection when multiple in-flight pages fail — the sliding window now always throws the **lowest-page-index** error; `RangeError` on spread-push with very large page counts (~120k+, reachable via `returnMetadataOnly`) — result array now returned directly; zero-copy guard now routes empty/detached buffers to the copy path.
  - **Fixed in tests:** parallel window test now uses `concurrencyLimit: 3` so the option wiring is provably distinct from the sequential constant; added zero-copy tests for the offset-0/partial-span and empty-buffer branches; added a test pinning sequential failure semantics (in-flight page completes, later pages never start, first-page error surfaces).
  - **Documented (accepted behavior deltas of the minor release, see below).**

## Behavioral notes (default/sequential mode)

Pixels, result order, and API defaults are unchanged, but three side-effect-level behaviors of the default mode change with pipelining:

1. **Disk writes may complete out of page order** (e.g. a fast page 3 can land before a slow page 2). Consume output via the resolved ordered `PngPageOutput[]`, not directory-watch order.
2. **On failure, the one page already in flight still completes** (including its write) before the promise rejects — on-disk output is no longer guaranteed to be a strict page-order prefix (bounded overshoot: at most one page).
3. **Peak canvas memory is up to two live canvases** instead of one. Escape hatch for strict one-at-a-time processing: `processPagesInParallel: true` + `concurrencyLimit: 1` (a sliding window of exactly one page).

All three are documented in the `processPagesInParallel` JSDoc that ships with the package types.

## Follow-ups (out of scope, found during investigation)

- **Image-heavy pages** (`large_pdf`-class): 85% of time sits in pdf.js main-thread image work (`convertRGBToRGBA`, JS JPEG decode) — unreachable in-process. A worker-thread page-level pool is the only route to big wins there; proposal with numbers to follow separately.
- `src/outputWriter.ts` performs two identical `realpath` calls per written page (`dirname(file)` ≡ output folder due to the flat-name guard); consolidating would save a syscall per page but touches the SEC-001/002/003 guard block — left untouched deliberately.
- `package.json` contains a duplicate `"overrides"` key (pre-existing).

## Summary

Introduces `apps.content` — the shared architectural foundation for all managed storefront destinations (menus, banners, hero slides, CTAs).

## Architecture

### DestinationMixin (Abstract Model)

Reusable FK-based destination supporting:
- Category (FK to catalog.Category)
- Product (FK to catalog.Product)
- Brand (FK to catalog.Brand)
- External URL (validated)
- None (no link)

### Safety

- **Model-level validation** (`clean()`) ensures exactly one destination matches the selected type
- **No GenericForeignKey** (preserves referential integrity)
- **No raw internal URL strings** (uses FK + named route resolution)
- **Deleted destinations** → `SET_NULL` → resolver returns `None`
- **External URL scheme allowlist**: `https`, `http`, `mailto`, `tel` only
- **Rejected**: `javascript:`, `data:`, `vbscript:`, `//...`

### Resolver Service

`resolve_destination_url(instance)` → `str | None`
- Never returns `#`
- Never fabricates paths
- Returns `None` for deleted/invalid destinations

## Summary

- remove `knowledge.semantic_search.*` from operator-owned `config.yaml`
- make the existing Knowledge settings API/UI the authoritative typed, tenant-scoped policy surface

- keep workspace-admin authorization and Postgres RLS / SQLite-static behavior aligned

## Migration and defaults

- legacy top-level `knowledge:` YAML is rejected with guidance to use workspace Knowledge settings
- a workspace with no stored policy resolves to semantic search disabled and the existing semantic defaults
- absent patch fields preserve current values; `null` resets supported policy fields or sections to defaults
- the repository stores only non-default typed policy overrides; after the first mutation, an empty policy row remains as the stable per-tenant mutation lock
- no database migration is required because this uses the established tenant-scoped, RLS-protected `app_variables` table
- existing encrypted `knowledge.embeddings/api_key` values remain in place; blank UI input preserves the key and the explicit removal action clears it
- Postgres/pgvector availability remains an operator/infrastructure capability rather than tenant policy

## Follow-up

Required-from-auth deployments still need a separate all-tenant background indexer discovery design. This PR deliberately does not conflate that work: the singleton startup indexer continues to drain only the startup/bootstrap tenant, although other tenants can safely configure policy and queue work without leaking settings or status across tenants.

Independent Codex review prompted two focused follow-up commits.

Commit `4656b5af`:

- models singleton settings/status/reindex client signatures exactly and removes UI casts
- centralizes supported OpenAI embedding models and portable policy invariants in core
- serializes first credential writes and makes settings plus dependent unit rebuilds atomic
- stamps internal app-variable inserts with the active tenant for Postgres RLS

Commit `c0c5565f`:

- uses the tenant policy row as a stable aggregate lock for every settings mutation and returns the locked previous/saved combined state for dependent unit updates
- schedules indexer wakes only after commit and detaches inherited database and operation tenant scopes; rollback drops the wake
- exposes `indexing.paused` in the settings UI so unrelated saves preserve it
- adds wake commit/rollback/scope tests, paused-policy UI coverage, and conditional Postgres concurrent credential/policy coverage


Commit `2d175545`:

- extends the stable aggregate guard to document/unit writes and manual reindex, with explicit SQLite immediate transactions and the existing Postgres tenant transaction
- reacquires the guard after provider work and validates policy, credential, unit identity, and content hash before committing embeddings or error status
- preserves wake requests arriving during an active indexer tick through a rerun flag
- adds deterministic Postgres guard-blocking coverage, SQLite document/reindex coordination tests, stale materialization-snapshot validation, and active-tick wake coverage


Commit `72ee341a`:

- brands aggregate-lock and in-transaction patch inputs as `TenantScopedDatabase`, encoding the active-transaction requirement in core signatures
- centralizes Knowledge policy transaction, SQLite immediate-lock retry, and ambient Postgres reuse in one daemon helper
- binds document materialization directly to the scoped transaction while avoiding the aggregate guard for metadata-only document writes
- passes the exact scoped database through indexer aggregate-lock callbacks
